newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi upbeat on Italy's economy and EMU chances.
newsitem.headline: Prodi upbeat on Italy's economy and EMU chances.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi tried to reassure gloomy industrialists on Thursday that economic recovery was on the way and Italy was winning its battle to meet tough economic criteria for a single European currency.

Prodi told business leaders gathered at the annual meeting of the Italian employers' federation Confindustria he saw the first signs of an economic upturn and that all conditions were in place for a cut in interest rates by the Bank of Italy.
"Today we are seeing the first signals of an economic recovery. We have attained certain conditions so that this upturn can finally take off," he said.
"We have defeated inflation which has fallen from 4.3 percent a year ago to 1.5 percent (in May)...There are now all the conditions for a reduction in interest rates."

Italy is battling to slash its budget deficit by the end of this year in order to join the first wave of nations in a single European currency under economic and monetary union (EMU) at the start of 1999.

EMU qualifications include a budget deficit target of no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP). Italy's deficit totalled 6.7 percent of GDP in 1996 but is falling fast as the government imposes a stringent tax squeeze.

Prodi, whose centre-left coalition government has forced through nearly 80 trillion lire ($48 billion) of deficit-trimming measures in the last six months, told industrialists: "As for the deficit/GDP ratio, today we are at 3.0 percent."
Lower interest rates would help the government's efforts to cut spending by bringing down the interest bill on Italy's debt mountain.
The Bank of Italy, determined to rid the country of its reputation for high inflation, has also kept a tight rein on monetary policy despite a sharp slowdown in inflation in the past year.

Preliminary May consumer prices data released this week show price growth running at 1.5 percent a year, its lowest since 1969. But real interest rates are nearer five percent, more than double those in France or Germany.
Financial markets believe it is only a matter of days before the central bank lowers the official discount rate, now at 6.75 percent, by up to three quarters of a percentage point.
Italian industry, which has been clamouring for months for lower borrowing costs, attributes the fall in inflation to economic stagnation and a stronger lira.

Confindustria chairman Giorgio Fossa warned the government not to count on "a vigorous, spontaneous recovery in the economy" as it mapped out its economic goals for the next three years, saying such a recovery did not seem probable.

Fossa told the Confindustria meeting not to underrate the risk of an upturn in inflation despite a sluggish economy. While Italy had managed to get near the EMU deficit/GDP threshold, "this does not yet give any guarantees of stability."
Prodi, who has staked his reputation on taking Italy into a single currency at the start in 1999, said the government was working on cuts in welfare spending in its drive to join EMU.
"All the conditions are there for Italy to be in the leading group," he later told a separate meeting of the CISL trades union confederation.
"At the moment we are only missing one Maastricht parameter, that on debt which it is difficult to do anything about -- but a year ago we were out on four of the five criteria," he said.

The Maastricht Treaty criteria on EMU require a country's debt levels not to exceed 60 percent of GDP or to be making progress towards achieving the target. Italy's debt is currently around 121 percent. ($ = 1669 Italian Lire)
